summary:
ASTRA—Astronaut Health Intelligence and Monitoring System—is a research prototype developed by Team BLUE to bring astronaut health observations into one connected review workflow. It combines simulated vital signs, personal baselines, and cabin conditions in a mission-control dashboard.

BioMonitor streams physiological measurements, RiskWatch detects deviations from individual baselines, and SpaceHealth provides environmental context. ASTRA Copilot retrieves recorded evidence with source citations, while MissionCare supports human review, reports, shift handovers, and a historical timeline.

ASTRA addresses the challenge by helping users see what changed, understand the supporting evidence, and preserve observations for follow-up. This matters because isolated readings can miss the broader picture: a changing pulse becomes more informative when viewed alongside a personal baseline, recent activity, and cabin conditions.

Our working prototype demonstrates this connected workflow using explicitly simulated data and NASA-STD-3001 background references. It is not medically validated and performs no automated treatment. Our goal is clearer, traceable evidence for human-supervised astronaut health decisions.
details:
Project overview

ASTRA—Astronaut Health Intelligence and Monitoring System—is a software research prototype developed by Team BLUE: Rohith B and Sneha Prakasan. It brings physiological observations, personal baselines, environmental context, and human review into one connected workflow.

Our goal is to demonstrate how astronaut health information could become easier to interpret, trace, and communicate during space missions. ASTRA currently uses explicitly simulated measurements; it is not medically validated or connected to real astronaut sensors.

How it works

ASTRA connects five functional modules:

  • BioMonitor streams simulated heart rate, heart-rate variability, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, sleep duration, and hydration indicators.
  • RiskWatch compares measurements with individual baselines and applies statistical, temporal, and multivariate rules to identify deviations. Its scores are experimental engineering indicators, not clinical predictions.
  • SpaceHealth adds mission-scoped cabin conditions, recorded exercise activity, sleep context, and simulated radiation measurements.
  • ASTRA Copilot uses deterministic retrieval and response rules to explain recorded observations, identify supporting sources, and distinguish current measurements from historical alerts. It does not require an external language model to operate.
  • MissionCare supports human acknowledgement and review of alerts, evidence-preserving reports, PDF exports, shift handovers, and a combined historical timeline.

In our demonstration, a controlled anomaly changes simulated vital signs. RiskWatch detects the resulting deviation, Copilot retrieves the supporting evidence, and a reviewer records an observation and changes the alert’s review status.

Benefits and intended impact

Individual measurements can be difficult to interpret without context. ASTRA places observations alongside a person’s baseline, measurement timestamps, mission conditions, and previous events.

The intended benefit is a clearer review process: users can see what changed, inspect why an alert appeared, identify missing or stale information, and preserve evidence for follow-up. Reports and handovers help maintain continuity between reviewers.

We envision this approach supporting future research into crew health awareness and mission health workflows. Actual operational use would require sensor integration, authenticated access, further reliability testing, and formal clinical and operational validation.

Technology and resources

The backend uses Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLAlchemy, and Alembic. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Recharts. REST APIs and WebSockets connect the interface to the backend. SQLite provides the verified local database; Docker and PostgreSQL configurations are prepared, but their runtime has not been verified.

The prototype runs on a conventional computer without dedicated hardware. Its simulator generates physiological and cabin measurements and supports controlled anomaly scenarios.

NASA-STD-3001 Volumes 1 and 2 are background references. We did not ingest original NASA astronaut measurement datasets or use these documents to establish clinically validated thresholds.

Creativity and design considerations

ASTRA’s creative contribution is the connection between personal baselines, mission context, explainable deviations, source provenance, and human review. Rather than presenting an isolated alert, it carries supporting observations through explanation, review, reporting, and handover.

We considered:

  • Individual differences: comparisons use stored personal baselines.
  • Data integrity: astronaut and mission records remain correctly associated; duplicate telemetry is rejected.
  • Scientific honesty: synthetic data is labeled, and missing or stale measurements remain visible.
  • Traceability: alert evidence and generated report snapshots are preserved as new measurements arrive.
  • Human authority: ASTRA performs no automated treatment or flight-readiness decision.
  • Reliability: the current software passes 77 backend tests, 28 frontend tests, and the production frontend build. These results verify software behavior, not medical effectiveness.
  • Access limitations: the verified deployment is a trusted local demonstration; authentication and role-based access remain future work.

SI-assisted development

OpenAI Codex assisted with software implementation, testing, documentation, narration scripting, and video-editing code. The demonstration uses recorded interactions with the working prototype, alongside SI-assisted titles and captions. Its narration was generated using ElevenLabs. Simulated measurements are produced by the prototype’s software generator and are not observations of real astronauts.

ASTRA is an independent research prototype and does not claim NASA endorsement, medical certification, or spaceflight qualification.
